name: Matthew (traditional attribution)
summary: The Gospel is anonymous; the title 'According to Matthew' was attached by the early second century. Papias (c. AD 110, quoted by Eusebius) says Matthew 'compiled the sayings in the Hebrew dialect'. Most modern scholars think the Greek Gospel we have was written c. AD 70–90 by a Jewish-Christian author using Mark, not directly by the tax collector; the attribution is early and unanimous but not self-attested.

sources.note: the call of Matthew the tax collector

traditions: Apostolic authorship: traditional Catholic, Orthodox and evangelical view
Anonymous Jewish-Christian author dependent on Mark: majority of critical scholarship

name: Mark (John Mark), from Peter's preaching
summary: Papias, via Eusebius, says Mark was Peter's 'interpreter' and wrote down what Peter taught, 'though not in order'. The Gospel itself is anonymous. Its Latinisms and explanations of Jewish customs suggest a Roman or at least non-Judean audience; most date it c. AD 65–75.
traditions: Broad agreement across traditions on the Papias account; date debated

name: Luke, companion of Paul
summary: Luke–Acts is a single two-volume work addressed to Theophilus. Its author is unnamed but the 'we' passages in Acts place him with Paul; tradition since the second century identifies him with 'Luke the beloved physician' of Colossians 4:14. The Muratorian fragment and Irenaeus both name him.
traditions: Lukan authorship widely accepted; some critical scholars regard the 'we' passages as a literary device

name: 'The disciple whom Jesus loved'
summary: The Gospel claims to rest on the testimony of the beloved disciple (21:24), whom it never names. Irenaeus identifies him with John the apostle, writing at Ephesus; some ancient and modern readers have proposed another John ('the Elder' whom Papias mentions). The final chapter's 'we know that his testimony is true' implies an editorial circle.

sources.title: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.39.4 (Papias on 'John the Elder')

traditions: John the Elder or a Johannine school: many critical scholars (e.g. Bauckham argues for John the Elder as an eyewitness)

name: Moses (traditional attribution of the Torah)
summary: The Pentateuch itself says Moses wrote specific things — the covenant words, the law, a song — and later Scripture calls the whole 'the Book of Moses'. The books are anonymous as wholes and narrate Moses' death. Jewish and Christian tradition holds Mosaic authorship; critical scholarship since the eighteenth century sees the Torah as composed from several sources and edited after the exile. Both agree the material is much older than its final form.

sources.note: Moses' death narrated in the third person

sources.title: Prolegomena to the History of Israel
sources.author: Julius Wellhausen
sources.note: the classic statement of the documentary hypothesis

traditions: Mosaic authorship: Orthodox Judaism, traditional Catholic and evangelical teaching
Composite authorship (J, E, D, P or successive editions): mainstream academic biblical studies

name: David (psalm superscriptions)
summary: 73 psalms carry the heading 'of David' (le-David). The Hebrew preposition can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to the collection of', so the headings attest an early tradition rather than settle authorship. The New Testament cites Psalms 2, 16, 32, 69, 95, 109 and 110 as David's. Other named contributors are Asaph (12), the sons of Korah (11), Solomon (2), Moses (1), Heman and Ethan (1 each).
traditions: Headings as later collection labels: most critical scholarship, which still allows Davidic origin for some psalms

name: Paul of Tarsus
summary: Thirteen letters name Paul as sender. Seven are accepted as his by virtually everyone (Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, Philemon). Ephesians, Colossians and 2 Thessalonians are debated; the Pastorals (1–2 Timothy, Titus) are held by most critical scholars to be by a later follower, on grounds of vocabulary, church structure and chronology. Paul dictated to a secretary (Romans 16:22) and signed in his own hand (Galatians 6:11).

sources.note: Paul's letters already collected and called 'Scriptures'

traditions: All thirteen Pauline: traditional and evangelical view
Seven undisputed, six deutero-Pauline: majority critical view

name: Isaiah of Jerusalem (and the question of chapters 40–66)
summary: Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem c. 740–700 BC (1:1). Chapters 40–66 address the Babylonian exile and name Cyrus (44:28; 45:1), events 150 years later; since the eighteenth century most scholars attribute them to one or two later prophets writing in Isaiah's tradition ('Second' and 'Third Isaiah'). Traditional readers take the Cyrus passages as predictive. The Great Isaiah Scroll (c. 125 BC) already has all 66 chapters as one book.

sources.title: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ), Shrine of the Book
Sirach 48:22–25 (c. 180 BC)
sources.note: already credits Isaiah with comforting 'those who mourned in Zion' — chapters 40–66

traditions: Single author: traditional Jewish and Christian view, conservative evangelicalism
Two or three authors: mainstream academic view, also accepted by many Catholic and mainline Protestant scholars

name: Hebrews: author unknown
summary: The letter names no author. Origen's verdict, 'who wrote the epistle, in truth God knows', has held for eighteen centuries. Candidates proposed since antiquity include Paul, Barnabas (Tertullian), Apollos (Luther), Luke, Clement of Rome and Priscilla (Harnack). Its polished Greek and its use of the Septuagint distinguish it from Paul's letters.
